children: By Gavin Maguire

Energy markets spent much of this year pricing in the possibility that conflict in the Middle East could spread and threaten fuel supplies, transport routes and energy security. Now that premium appears to be going into reverse.
Since the US midterm elections, a broad range of energy-linked markets — from crude oil, diesel and tanker rates to natural gas, LNG and coal — have moved lower together.
Each market has its own fundamentals. Yet the synchronized nature of the retreat suggests investors are reassessing something larger than oil balances, gas inventories or coal demand.
What appears to be changing is the perceived risk of a wider Middle East conflict.
A NEW WORST-CASE SCENARIO?

Energy traders appear to be reassessing the probability of a wider regional conflict following the US midterm elections, which shifted market expectations toward a potentially more diplomatic US foreign policy stance.
The

to the Democrats signals a greater likelihood that Washington will pursue diplomatic engagement and negotiated settlements across multiple geopolitical flashpoints, including the conflicts that have kept risk premiums elevated throughout global energy markets this year.

Whether such efforts ultimately deliver lasting peace is almost beside the point. Markets trade expectations, not outcomes, and what appears to have changed since the election is the perceived probability of the most disruptive scenarios.

Before the vote, markets appeared to be assigning a higher probability to scenarios involving further escalation, threatening oil exports from the Gulf, disrupting key shipping routes, tightening LNG supplies and raising freight costs.
Those concerns helped push crude oil, diesel, natural gas, LNG and tanker rates higher in tandem.
Since the election, investors appear to be marking down those risks.
SHIPPING SIGNALS

One of the clearest signals comes from tanker markets, which tend to react immediately to changes in perceived security risks. Freight costs on key Middle East export routes have fallen sharply since the election result.
Rates for chartering a very large crude carrier (VLCC) from the Middle East to China have slumped to roughly $1 million per day currently from over $1.4 million a day in October, according to LSEG.
Those rates remain hugely elevated compared to the rate of around $200,000 a day just prior to the conflict, but still indicate a rapid loosening of tensions compared to a few weeks ago.
Shipping costs tend to react quickly to concerns over security risks, insurance costs, route disruptions and vessel availability.
Since the US midterm election results, freight markets appear to be factoring in a lower probability of disruptions along key export corridors.

That matters because tanker rates often function as a real-time measure of geopolitical anxiety. When traders become more or less concerned about threats to shipping, freight markets frequently respond before broader commodity fundamentals change.
The recent retreat in tanker costs therefore reinforces the notion that investors are unwinding a geopolitical premium rather than responding solely to changing supply and demand balances.
OIL DRAG
Crude oil prices are another telltale sign of dissipating risks.

Crude remains the anchor market for the wider energy system. When perceived geopolitical risk falls, oil prices tend to fall first, while refined products such as diesel and gasoline generally follow.

Brent crude oil futures traded around $115 per barrel at the end of October, but have since retreated to below $95 a barrel on a recovery in crude oil export volumes from the Middle East and expectations that the global oil market will return to a surplus by the end of the year.

In combination, recovering export volumes and expectations of a year-end surplus have given traders fundamental justification to shed some of the insurance premium built into prices during the conflict.
European diesel futures (LGOZ6), which scaled record highs above $1,450 per metric ton in September, are also on the downslope, and currently trade at around $1,220 a ton.
US diesel futures have also retreated sharply from recent record highs, and are currently trading around $4.08 a gallon compared to around $4.80 a gallon just prior to the midterms.
COOLER COAL, JITTERY GAS

Coal prices are less directly connected to Middle East politics, but even coal can benefit from periods of elevated energy security concerns. And when fears recede, support for coal prices can weaken as well.
Benchmark thermal coal (CMAP2c1) prices in Europe were trading around $146 per ton shortly before the US midterms, and are now around $10 a ton lower.
Futures on coal exported from Newcastle in Australia have undergone a similar decline, to around $145 a ton currently from around $150 a ton just prior to the midterms.
But the unwinding of risk premiums does not mean all energy markets suddenly look comfortable.
Europe's gas market remains particularly vulnerable, even though prices have also trended steadily lower since the midterm results.
Benchmark futures for the Dutch trading hub
were trading just shy of €104 per megawatt hour on October 30, but are now holding around €84/MWh as the broad de-risking across energy markets tugged gas lower.
But Europe's gas markets are certainly not out of the woods given that the peak period for gas demand is still ahead.
Europe's gas inventories are currently around 70% of storage capacity, according to data from LSEG, compared to an average of  around 89% full for this time of year since 2020.
Further, utilities are already into the stock-depleting period of the year as heating demand picks up, and so will likely trigger additional stock draws during any cold spells.
FUNDAMENTALS BACK IN FOCUS
The broad decline across multiple fuel markets in recent days is likely the result of the unwinding of a single macro trade.
With much of that geopolitical risk premium now reduced, individual market fundamentals are again driving price direction.

Weather remains an important risk. So does the possibility of unplanned outages at LNG export facilities and the reduced flexibility for European gas buyers after years of drawing down Russian pipeline supplies.
Those structural issues have not disappeared simply because geopolitical risk perceptions have eased.
The same applies to oil.

The Middle East remains responsible for a large share of global crude exports. Shipping routes through the region remain critical for both oil and LNG trade. A fresh escalation in hostilities involving major producers or export terminals would rapidly rebuild the risk premium now being removed.
But Europe's gas market serves as a reminder that not every premium has vanished. Some risks remain stubbornly real.
The difference is that traders are once again paying more attention to actual supply threats than hypothetical ones. That alone marks a significant change in the market's outlook.
